title: Defensive design considerations
starter: Think of three ways someone could get into a school computer account without ever breaking the software. How could the school stop each one?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Anticipating misuse
facts: Thinking ahead about how users might accidentally or deliberately misuse a program.
E.g. typing text where a number is expected, or clicking a button many times.
stations.challenge: List three ways a user might misuse a program that asks for their age.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Thinking ahead about how users might accidentally or deliberately misuse a program.
Also credit: E.g. typing text where a number is expected, or clicking a button many times.

questions.a: Planning for the ways users might accidentally or deliberately misuse a program

questions.q: A user types their name into a box asking for a number. What should a robust program do?
questions.a: Reject it with a helpful message and ask again

stations.name: When things go wrong
facts: Even with valid input, a program can crash: dividing by zero, a lost connection, a printer out of paper, or a full disk.
Programmers use exception handling so the program copes instead of crashing.
stations.challenge: Fill in the four problems shown on the wall.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Even with valid input, a program can crash: dividing by zero, a lost connection, a printer out of paper, or a full disk.
Also credit: Programmers use exception handling so the program copes instead of crashing.

questions.q: Which of these could crash a program even when the input is valid? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Dividing by zero; The network connection dropping; The printer running out of paper; The storage being full

questions.q: How can a program cope with a problem like a missing file?
questions.a: Exception handling: catching the error and responding sensibly

stations.name: Authentication
facts: Checking a user is who they say they are before they can use a system.
Strong passwords are long and mix upper and lower case, numbers and symbols.
stations.challenge: Explain the difference between validation and authentication.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Checking a user is who they say they are before they can use a system.
Also credit: Usually a username and password.

questions.a: Checking a user's identity before they can use a system

stations.name: Forgotten passwords and new users
facts: A reset link or code can be sent to a registered email address or phone.
New users often confirm their email address before the account is activated.
Two-factor authentication adds a code sent to your phone.
stations.challenge: Why is a reset link sent to your email, not shown on screen?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A reset link or code can be sent to a registered email address or phone.
Also credit: New users often confirm their email address before the account is activated.

questions.q: Why does a website email a link to reset your password?
questions.a: Only the real owner should be able to access that email account
Using a second check, such as a code sent to your phone, as well as a password

stations.name: Bots and CAPTCHA
facts: Bots are programs that fill in forms automatically, e.g. to make fake accounts or guess passwords.
CAPTCHA tests like 'I'm not a robot' are easy for humans but hard for bots.
Audio CAPTCHAs help users who can't see the images.
stations.challenge: Why would an attacker want a program that fills in forms automatically? Suggest two ways a website can stop one.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Bots are programs that fill in forms automatically, e.g. to make fake accounts or guess passwords.
Also credit: CAPTCHA tests like 'I'm not a robot' are easy for humans but hard for bots.

questions.q: What is a CAPTCHA used for?
questions.a: Stopping automated bots from using a form

questions.q: How are CAPTCHAs made accessible to people who can't see images?

stations.name: Validate a password
facts: It must be at least 10 characters long.
It must contain a digit and a letter.
It must not be one of the 100 most common passwords.
stations.challenge: Write the first three lines of a password validation program.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: It must be at least 10 characters long.
Also credit: It must contain a digit and a letter.

questions.q: Which passwords pass all three rules? Select all that apply.
Why does the program use strip() on the input first?
questions.a: It removes spaces typed by accident at the start or end

final.name: Final challenge: defend the program

questions.q: Is each defence validation, authentication or anticipating misuse?
questions.a: A username and password login = Authentication; A code sent to your phone = Authentication; Checking an age is between 11 and 19 = Validation; Checking an email contains an @ = Validation; Not crashing when the printer runs out of paper = Misuse; Handling a user dividing by zero = Misuse; Checking a field isn't left empty = Validation; Confirming a new account from an email link = Authentication

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by authentication, using an example.
points: Two-factor authentication adds a code sent to your phone.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Describe two techniques a website can use to stop automated programs creating accounts.
points: Bots are programs that fill in forms automatically, e.g. to make fake accounts or guess passwords.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: A program divides one number by another entered by the user. Explain how the programmer should handle a division by zero.

E.g. typing text where a number is expected, or clicking a button many times.

Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
